cover.headline: Telangana's leading hospital chain, mid-way through a five-state build-out: the market already pays for the new beds to fill
cover.lead: KIMS runs 26 multi-specialty hospitals (7,459 beds, 5,639 operational) at tier-2 prices: its mature hospitals in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh earn 25-30% EBITDA margins at an ARPOB of ₹47,200, a fraction of metro chains'. Since FY24 it has added ~3,500 beds in four new states, which cut the FY26 margin to 21% (new units lost ₹128 cr), pushed net debt to 5.4x EBITDA and forced a ₹1,500 cr QIP and ₹600 cr of promoter warrants in Jun-Aug 2026. Q1FY27 revenue rose 35%, EBITDA 16%; profit fell 47%. The street values KIMS on **EV/EBITDA on FY28E (27-30x)**. We forecast EBITDA of ₹1,057 / 1,366 / 1,716 cr and EPS of ₹6.5 / 11.4 / 16.6 for FY27-29E (42.77 cr fully diluted shares). Applying **19.5x to Sep-28E EBITDA of ₹1,541 cr** (post-Ind AS; leases and minorities in net debt) gives **{{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}})**: **we initiate with SELL.** Cross-checks: P/E ₹533, DCF ₹579. Bull case {{scen.bull.tp|inr}}; bear case {{scen.bear.tp|inr}}.

arguments.p: Telangana (half of revenue, ~77% of EBITDA in Q1FY27) earns ~30% margins and Andhra Pradesh 21-25% at an ARPOB of only ~₹25,000. Doctor-partners own equity in ten hospital companies, which helps recruitment but leaks profit to minorities (₹30 cr in FY25).

arguments.h: The new hospitals are turning, one by one
arguments.p: Nashik broke even and Mahadevapura turned positive in Q1FY27; Bengaluru's loss halved to ₹19 cr; Electronic City (−₹18 cr) and Thane (−₹7 cr) are next. We assume new-unit losses fall from ₹128 cr to ₹60 cr in FY27E and model revenue +{{F.salesGrowth.0|pct}} / +{{F.salesGrowth.1|pct}} / +{{F.salesGrowth.2|pct}} from a five-cluster build.

arguments.h: Repaired with equity, not cash flow
arguments.p: Net debt including leases and minorities was ₹4,386 cr at Mar-26 (5.4x EBITDA); the QIP and warrants (7% dilution) cut it to ~₹2,310 cr pro forma. Promoters pledged another 6.67% of the company on 18-Sep-2026, and management plans new greenfields from FY28. Our margin ({{F.ebitdaMargin.1|pct}} in FY28E) is below PL and Axis.

arguments.h: Valuation: the recovery is in the price
arguments.p: At ₹746 KIMS trades at 25.1x our FY28E EV/EBITDA, above its 21.8x forward median since listing, while hospital peers sit ~11% below their own medians. 19.5x on Sep-28E gives ₹660; the street's 27-30x would be ₹818-914. P/E and DCF are lower still.

catalysts: Q2FY27 results (due by mid-November 2026): the first quarter with lower interest after the QIP repayments, Thane and Electronic City breakeven, Kondapur's ramp and Bengaluru's path to an EBITDA-neutral year.
Thrissur O&M hospital (351 beds) due within 3-4 months of Aug-2026; Secunderabad replacement block by end-CY27; Rajahmundry II under construction.
Call options on O&M hospitals exercisable from Jan-2027, and the new greenfield or acquisition projects management expects to announce in FY28.
Conversion of the promoter warrants (₹450 cr due within 18 months of Aug-2026) and any further change in promoter pledges.
Insurer empanelment of Thane, Nashik and the Bengaluru hospitals (key panels expected by mid-September 2026).

sections.title: Multi-specialty hospitals at tier-2 prices, built in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, now in five states

blocks.p: KIMS runs general multi-specialty hospitals that do complex (tertiary) work: cardiac surgery, neurosurgery, joint replacement, kidney care, gastroenterology, cancer care and heart, lung, liver and kidney transplants. Its formula, set by the founder Dr B. Bhaskara Rao (a cardio-thoracic surgeon who helped design Andhra Pradesh's Aarogyasri health scheme in 2007), is big hospitals at "affordable" prices in second-tier cities, run with full-time doctors, many of whom own equity in the local hospital company. Revenue per occupied bed-day (ARPOB) was ₹47,200 in Q1FY27, far below metro chains, yet the mature Telangana hospitals earn ~30% EBITDA margins.

In FY26 hospital services brought in ₹2,653 cr, pharmacy ₹1,202 cr and other income from operations (academic courses, food, O&M fees) ₹49 cr. Cash-paying patients are 52% of revenue, insurers 32%, corporates and government health plans (CGHS, PSUs) 12% and the Aarogyasri scheme only 4% (Q1FY27). No single specialty dominates: cardiac and orthopaedics 15% each, neurosciences 11%, renal, gastro and mother & child 9% each, oncology 7%, transplants 3%.

sections.title: A growing, under-bedded market, but the bed boom is now in KIMS's home city

blocks.p: ICRA's sample of listed and unlisted hospital chains (30-Jul-2026): revenue growth of 13-15% in FY27 and 15-17% in FY28, cut from 18-20% for FY27 in its Dec-2025 update; FY26 occupancy 63.5%; ARPOB +6-8% in FY27 after +9.2% in FY26; operating margin 22-24% in FY27-28 (24.1% in FY26); outlook Positive. ICRA (Jul-2025) expected the sector to add ~14,500 beds for ₹30,000-32,000 cr of capex by FY27. For KIMS three things matter more than the national average: competition for patients and doctors in Hyderabad, where several large hospitals opened in the last year; insurers' willingness to empanel new hospitals quickly, which slowed every one of KIMS's FY26 openings; and the price point of tier-2 Andhra Pradesh, where ARPOB is a third of Hyderabad's.

sections.title: Five clusters, two of them earning the money: Telangana and Andhra make all the EBITDA

blocks.p: Hospital revenue is operational beds × occupancy × ARPOB (revenue per occupied bed-day, which at KIMS includes outpatient and pharmacy revenue). The five clusters are very different businesses. **Telangana** (Hyderabad: Secunderabad, Kondapur, the two Sunshine hospitals) charges ~₹77,000 a bed-day and earns ~30%. **Andhra Pradesh** (eight hospitals in smaller towns) charges only ~₹25,000 and still earns 21-25%, the cheapest tertiary care in the listed sector. **Maharashtra** (Nagpur, Nashik, Thane), **Kerala** (Kannur, Kollam, Palakkad) and **Karnataka** (two Bengaluru hospitals) are 1-4 years old and earned nothing between them in FY26 (−₹88 cr of EBITDA).

blocks.callout: **What would move the numbers:** each 1pp of group occupancy on ~5,800 operational beds is ~58 occupied beds, or ~₹100 cr of revenue at FY27E ARPOB. Management's claim that Telangana's like-for-like occupancy is already 61-65% matters: the reported 41% in Q1FY27 is the enlarged Kondapur hospital starting nearly empty. Our build has group occupancy at 50.4% / 53.0% / 54.7% in FY27-29E on 5,800 / 6,310 / 6,830 operational beds; management talks of 65-70% by FY30 if no beds are added.

sections.title: The new hospitals cost ₹128 cr of EBITDA in FY26; Q1FY27 shows them turning, one by one

blocks.p: This is the central question for KIMS. In FY26 its mature hospitals earned ₹956 cr of EBITDA on ₹3,335 cr of revenue (~29%), while units in their first year lost ₹128 cr on ₹597 cr (FY25: −₹18.3 cr). Without those losses FY26 EBITDA would have been ~₹943 cr, up 19% rather than 3%. The good news in Q1FY27: Nashik broke even, Mahadevapura (Bengaluru) was EBITDA-positive from June, Vizag QNRI (acquired loss-making in 2024) reached a ~16% margin and Kerala made money. The bad news: Electronic City still lost ~₹18 cr in the quarter, Thane ~₹7 cr, and the 787-bed Kondapur hospital and Thrissur start the cycle again.

blocks.callout: **Our view:** the record of the last two years is mixed but improving: Nashik took about two years to break even, Mahadevapura 7-9 months, Thane longer than promised because insurers were slow to empanel it and Maharashtra doctors join part-time first. Management's FY27 promise (Bengaluru cluster EBITDA-neutral for the year) needs Electronic City to break even by the second half. sections.title: Pipeline: fill the beds already built, then O&M and a new round of greenfields

blocks.p: After adding ~3,500 beds in two and a half years, KIMS says the next eight months are about stabilising what it has built: filling the 787-bed Kondapur hospital (₹45 cr in July versus ₹32-33 cr a month at the old site; potential ~₹100 cr a month in 4-5 years), finishing the Secunderabad replacement block (end-CY27) and Rajahmundry II, and opening Thrissur under an O&M contract. It is also growing asset-light: in Aug-Sep 2026 it signed O&M agreements for Arete Hospital in Gachibowli (250 beds) and a 183-bed hospital in Kakinada, both for 9% of revenue, with options to buy later. New greenfield projects are likely to be announced in FY28, only in its existing states (plus one hospital in Chennai).

Advantage

blocks.callout: **Honest verdict:** in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh KIMS has a genuine advantage: dense networks, doctor loyalty built through equity partnerships, and a cost structure that earns 25-30% margins at prices well below the metro chains. That moat does **not** travel automatically. In Bengaluru, Thane and Kerala KIMS is a new entrant competing against established chains, and FY26 showed it lacks bargaining power with insurers for new hospitals. The low-price model is also a ceiling: KIMS's ARPOB is about half that of the metro-focused chains, so its margin upside comes from filling beds, not from price.

sections.title: Revenue tripled since FY21, but profit fell in FY26 as ten new hospitals opened

blocks.p: KIMS grew revenue from ₹1,330 cr in FY21 to ₹3,905 cr in FY26 (24% a year), with acquisitions (Sunshine and Nagpur in 2022, Vizag QNRI in 2024) and a five-state building programme. Margins tell the other half of the story: EBITDA was 32% of revenue in FY22 (a Covid-era peak), 26% in FY24-25 and only 20.9% in FY26, when Thane, two Bengaluru hospitals, Kerala and several O&M units opened in the same year and lost ₹128 cr of EBITDA between them. Profit attributable to shareholders fell 37% to ₹241 cr in FY26 because depreciation and interest on the new hospitals arrived before their revenue: depreciation rose from ₹177 cr to ₹283 cr and interest from ₹100 cr to ₹215 cr.

sections.title: Expansion paid for with debt, then with new shares: ₹2,400 cr of capex in two years

blocks.p: Over FY25-26 KIMS generated ₹1,093 cr of operating cash but spent ₹2,437 cr on capex, ₹176 cr on acquisitions and O&M deals, ₹250 cr buying out doctor-partners (mainly Sunshine), and ₹363 cr on interest and lease interest. The gap, ₹2,123 cr, was borrowed: bank debt rose from ₹1,047 cr (Mar-24) to ₹3,244 cr (Mar-26). Returns fell with it: ROCE (Screener) was 34% in FY22, 17% in FY24 and 10% in FY26. In June 2026 KIMS raised ₹1,500 cr in a QIP and in August its promoters subscribed to ₹600 cr of warrants; ₹1,125 cr of debt was repaid by early July. Management says the next three to four years of operating cash (₹2,000-2,500 cr) will go into new greenfield and brownfield hospitals in its existing states.

sections.title: Earnings quality: read the EBITDA definitions, the minorities and the related-party Kondapur structure

bullets: **Three EBITDA numbers.** The company's "EBITDA" includes other income (FY26 ₹828 cr, 21.1%); Screener's and ours excludes it (₹815 cr, 20.9%); both are post-Ind AS 116, i.e. before rent. Pre-Ind AS (after rent) it was ₹785 cr including other income. Rent is small for KIMS (₹44 cr in FY26) because it owns most hospitals, but rising (₹18 cr in Q1FY27).
**Doctors sit in other expenses.** Consultancy charges to doctors were ₹1,007 cr (25.8% of revenue) on top of ₹682 cr of employee cost.

**Capitalisation is unwinding.** In FY26 ₹34 cr of lease interest and ₹21.5 cr of right-of-use depreciation were capitalised into projects; as hospitals open these move into the P&L, which is why profit lags EBITDA in FY27.

**Minorities.** Ten hospital companies have doctor-partners (stakes 51-91%). Their share of profit fell from ₹30 cr (FY25) to ₹0.6 cr (FY26) because they share Bengaluru and Nashik losses; it rises again as those turn profitable (management: 10-15% of profit long term). We report profit attributable to owners throughout and count minorities at book (₹311 cr) in net debt.

**O&M accounting.** Kannur and Kollam are consolidated as business combinations (right-of-use assets, contingent consideration); Sangli, Guntur and Kompally earn a fee and sit outside the bed KPIs; call options on O&M hospital companies are fair-valued through P&L (−₹3.8 cr in FY26).
**One-offs.** FY25 included a ₹12 cr land sale in revenue and EBITDA and a ₹10.9 cr asset-sale gain; FY26 an ₹11.2 cr exceptional loss and a ₹46 cr deferred-tax credit.
**Cash conversion.** Operating cash flow was 63% of EBITDA in FY26 (73% in FY25) as receivables grew faster than revenue (52 days, from 28 in FY22).

**Related parties.** The new 787-bed Kondapur hospital building belongs to Kondapur Healthcare Ltd, a 40.5% associate that KIMS has also lent ₹68.8 cr (12%); who owns the other 59.5% is not disclosed in what we read. In FY25 KIMS sold land for ₹45 cr to a company of KMP relatives. Small in value, but they deserve scrutiny.

blocks.callout: **Accounting flag: AMBER.** Disclosure is good (cluster P&Ls every quarter, unit charts for new hospitals) and the auditor (S.R. Batliboi, EY) is clean. The amber is for structure: three EBITDA definitions in circulation, profit leaking to minorities, capitalised costs now unwinding, an associate-owned flagship building and slow receivables.

sections.title: Net debt peaked at 5.4x EBITDA in March 2026; the QIP and warrants cut it to ~2.8x

blocks.p: At March 2026 KIMS owed ₹3,244 cr to banks, had ₹1,009 cr of lease liabilities (leased hospitals in Kerala, Thane and Bengaluru, and right-of-use assets under the Kerala O&M agreements) and ₹311 cr of minority partners' equity in its subsidiaries, against only ₹178 cr of cash, funds and investments (including ₹88 cr in the associate that owns the new Kondapur building). That is net debt of ₹4,386 cr on our basis, 5.4x FY26 EBITDA. Adding the QIP proceeds (₹1,476 cr net) and all ₹600 cr of the warrant money gives a pro forma ₹2,310 cr, 2.8x FY26 and ~2.2x our FY27E EBITDA. The company reported debt of ₹2,570 cr at June 2026 and ~₹2,400 cr in early August (excluding leases), and targets ~2x net debt/EBITDA.

sections.title: Our honest summary: a good regional operator whose recovery is already in the price

blocks.callout: **What you are buying:** the leading hospital chain in Telangana and Andhra Pradesh, with mature hospitals earning 25-30% margins at low prices, ~3,500 new beds already built and starting to fill, a balance sheet repaired by ₹2,100 cr of new equity, and a founder family adding money through warrants.

**What you are paying:** 25.1x our FY28E EV/EBITDA and 65.4x FY28E EPS, above KIMS's own 21.8x forward EV/EBITDA median since listing at a time when hospital peers trade ~11% below theirs. On the street's method and our inputs the target is {{dcf.tp|inr}} ({{dcf.upside|chg}}): a SELL. The market is paying for the new hospitals to fill on schedule; KIMS's record (Thane, Electronic City) says some will be late.

exhibit.title: Terms used in this report
head: Term
What it means
rows: Complex hospital care (heart and brain surgery, transplants, cancer treatment) as opposed to routine (primary/secondary) care.
Beds built vs beds staffed and open. KIMS's operational beds include census beds (wards, ICUs) and non-census beds (day care, emergency, dialysis).
Average revenue per occupied bed-day: hospital revenue (incl. outpatients and pharmacy) ÷ occupied bed-days.
Average revenue per inpatient: hospital revenue ÷ number of inpatients. Management prefers it because it moves less with the length of stay.
Average length of stay: occupied bed-days ÷ inpatients.
KIMS's reporting unit: all hospitals in one state (Telangana, Andhra Pradesh, Maharashtra, Kerala, Karnataka).
Hospitals in their first year or so; the EBITDA they lose while filling up (₹128 cr in FY26).
KIMS runs a hospital owned by someone else, either for a fee (~9% of revenue) or, where it controls it, consolidating it; often with a call option to buy it later.
Approval by an insurer, government health plan (CGHS, ESIC, PSUs) or scheme to treat its members cashlessly. New hospitals need it to attract insured patients.
The Andhra Pradesh / Telangana state health scheme for poorer families (4-5% of KIMS's revenue).
A KIMS subsidiary in which local doctors own a minority stake (KIMS holds 51-91%).
The doctor-partners' share of those subsidiaries; their share of profit is not KIMS shareholders' profit.
Accounting rule that puts leased buildings on the balance sheet: rent is replaced by depreciation and interest, and future rent appears as a lease liability.
EBITDA after deducting rent (pre-Ind AS) vs before rent (post-Ind AS, as reported and on Screener).
Qualified institutional placement: new shares sold to institutional investors (KIMS: ₹1,500 cr at ₹755 in June 2026).
Rights to buy new shares at a fixed price (₹779) within 18 months; promoters paid 25% upfront.
Shares given as security for a loan; if the price falls the lender can sell them.
Enterprise value (market value plus net debt, here including lease liabilities and minorities) ÷ EBITDA; share price ÷ earnings per share.
Half of FY28E plus half of FY29E: the 12-month-forward earnings the market will look at in September 2027.
Discounted cash flow valuation; WACC is the required annual return used to discount future cash (here 11.3%).
